children.translated_text: First Canto
With a fierce sun and a longed-for moon,
with stores of water diminished by constant bathing,
delightful at the close of day, when desire has subsided,
this summer season (<s>nidāgha</s>) has arrived, O beloved.
Nights with their dark blue luster pierced by the moon,
here and there charming water-fountain pavilions,
jeweled ramparts and moist sandal-paste —
in summer, O beloved, these come to be enjoyed by people.
The fragrant upper terrace of the palace, enchanting,
wine stirred by the breath from the beloved's face,
the song of fine stringed instruments that kindles desire —
lovers enjoy these in the summer midnight.
With round hips girdled in fine silk,
with breasts adorned with necklaces and sandal-paste,
with tresses fragrant from the bath-infusion —
women allay the summer heat of their lovers.
With feet stained deep red with lac-dye,
of full-hipped women, [adorned] with anklets,
at every step imitating the cry of swans —
the mind of people is made full of desire.
Breasts anointed with sandal-paste,
crowned with necklaces white as snow,
and hip-regions with golden girdles —
whose mind do they not make eager?
With sweat arising at the joints of their limbs,
discarding heavy garments now,
upon their breasts, those high-breasted young women
place only a thin cloth.
By breezes from fans sprinkled with sandal-water,
by [the touch of] necklace-strands upon the breast-circles,
by the sounds of the <s>vallakī</s> (lute) and <s>kākalī</s> song —
desire, as if asleep, is now awakened.
Upon the white terraces, at night, the moon,
seeing the happily sleeping faces of women,
surely grows intensely eager for a long time,
and at the end of night fades to pallor, as if from shame.
With dust-clouds raised by unbearable winds,
scorched by the blazing sun's heat, the earth
cannot even be looked upon by travelers
whose minds are burnt by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
Deer, intensely tormented by the fierce sun's heat,
their palates parched with great thirst,
rush into the forest interior [thinking] 'Water!'
seeing the sky [dark] like split collyrium.
With playful, smiling, sidelong glances,
graceful women in the minds of travelers
quickly kindle the fire of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the Bodiless One, Kāma),
just as the early evenings adorned with the beautiful moon.
Intensely scorched by the sun's rays,
burned on the path by hot sand,
with downcast face, crooked gait, panting repeatedly,
the serpent sits beneath the peacock's [spread] tail.
His vigor and effort overcome by great thirst,
panting repeatedly, mouth gaping wide,
the lion does not kill the elephants even nearby —
his tongue lolling, the tips of his mane trembling.
With spray-drops rising from their dried-out throats,
tormented by the rays of the sun,
stricken by overwhelming thirst, seeking water,
the elephants do not fear even the lions.
By the sun's rays like sacrificial fire,
the peacocks, body and mind exhausted,
do not kill the nearby serpent
that has placed its face within the circle of their tail-fans.
Digging in the lake [now] with dried mud and <s>bhadramusta</s> grass,
with its extended herd of snouts,
intensely tormented by the sun's rays,
a herd of boars seems to enter the earth itself.
Scorched by the sun with its most piercing garland of rays
from the lake with its muddy water,
a frog, leaping up, sits beneath
the hood-parasol of a thirsty serpent.
Stripped of all its networks of lotus-stalks,
its fish perished, its <s>sārasa</s> cranes fled in fear,
the lake is trampled to dense mud
by elephants pressing against each other.
Its crest-jewel split open by the sun's rays,
the wind licked by its twin flickering tongues,
tormented by the fire of venom, the sun, and heat, the serpent,
bewildered by thirst, does not strike the frog-clan.
With mouths covered in foamy saliva,
faces upturned with reddish tongues protruding,
bewildered by thirst, emerging from mountain caves,
the buffalo herds look about for water.
With crop-sprouts dried up by the sharp, scorching heat,
with parched leaves blown away by the force of rough winds,
with waters diminished on all sides by the sun's heat —
the forest interiors, when beheld, instill great fear.
The flocks of birds pant on trees with fallen leaves;
the monkey tribes, exhausted, retreat to mountain groves;
herds of <s>gavaya</s> (wild cattle) wander everywhere seeking water;
the <s>śarabha</s> (eight-legged beast) herds draw water straight up from wells.
With a blaze bright as blooming <s>kusumbha</s> and fresh vermillion,
swiftly driven by the force of powerful winds,
wildly embracing the tips of trees and creepers on the bank,
the lands in every direction are burned by wildfire.
Augmented by wind, it blazes in mountain caves,
it crackles with sharp sounds in groves of dry bamboo,
it spreads through the grass, growing in an instant —
the forest fire, reaching the borders, exhausts the herds of deer.
Seeming to multiply in the forests of <s>śālmalī</s> (silk-cotton) trees,
flashing gold-bright in the hollows of trees,
leaping up to tall trees with their branches of mature leaves,
the fire, driven by wind, wanders everywhere at the forest's edge.
Elephants, wild cattle, and lions, their bodies scorched by fire,
come together like friends, abandoning their mutual enmity;
quickly emerging from the thickets, weary of the fire,
they enter the broad sandy banks of a river.
With water fragrant from lotus-beds, delightful with the pink of <s>pāṭala</s> [flowers],
with pleasant sprinkling of water, wearing garlands of moonbeams to be enjoyed,
may your summer pass, accompanied by beautiful women,
happily on the palace-top, with lovely songs in the night.
Second Canto
With clouds spraying mist, elephants in rut,
with lightning as its banner, thunder as its drum,
it has arrived like a king, with upraised splendor —
this rainy season (<s>ghanāgama</s>), dear to lovers, O beloved.
With hues [dark] as the petals of deep blue lotuses,
here like heaps of split collyrium,
here like the breasts of a pregnant woman,
the sky is covered everywhere with clouds.
Beseeched by the <s>cātaka</s> birds bewildered by thirst,
hanging heavy with their load of water,
the rain-clouds move slowly, showering in many streams,
with sounds delightful to the ears and mind.
The rain-clouds, with thunder as their drums,
bearing <s>Indra</s>'s bow with its string of lightning,
with fierce arrows of sharp torrential rain,
pierce forcibly the hearts of travelers.
Covered with shoots of grass like split emerald,
strewn with risen <s>kandalī</s> leaves,
the earth, adorned with dark-colored jewels,
shines like a beautiful woman [adorned] with <s>indragopa</s> insects.
Always charming, eager with the festival of [their own] cries,
adorned with widely spread, beautiful tail-fans,
agitated by eager embraces and kisses,
the peacock clan has begun its dance today.
Toppling the trees along their banks,
with increased force of turbid waters,
like very wicked women wild with passion,
the rivers rush swiftly to the ocean.
With heaps of grass from which tender shoots have sprouted,
strewn with blue [flowers] nibbled by doe-faced [deer],
the <s>Vindhya</s> forests captivate the mind,
adorned with trees bearing fresh leaves.
With deer, alarmed on all sides,
whose faces are lovely with trembling water-lily eyes,
the sandy forest-glades
produce eagerness in the mind.
Though the rain-cloud rumbles loudly again and again
and the nights are made dense with darkness,
with lightning illuminating the path before them,
women go to their trysts (<s>abhisārikās</s>), driven by passion.
By the terrifying, deep rumbling of the rain-clouds,
by lightning, their minds greatly agitated,
women embrace their lovers in bed without interruption,
even those who have offended them.
With tears [falling] like water-drops from blue-lotus eyes,
with lovely lower lips like <s>bimba</s>-fruit [drenched],
having cast aside garlands, ornaments, and unguents,
the wives of travelers stand without hope.
Pale, bearing insect-dust and grass,
creeping with crooked motion like a snake,
watched with alarm by frog-clans,
the new rainwater flows toward the lowlands.
Eagerly abandoning the lotus-pond whose flowers have fallen,
the bees with ear-charming hum,
confused, fall upon the tail-fans
of the dancing peacocks, mistaking them for fresh blue lotuses.
Of forest elephants, intoxicated,
trumpeting again and again at the sounds of fresh rain-clouds,
their temple-regions, lustrous as pure blue lotuses,
are covered with swarms of bees [attracted by] the rut-fluid.
With rocks [dark] like white-lotus-hued clouds,
surrounded everywhere by cascading streams,
crowded with dancing peacocks,
the mountains generate eagerness in people.
Shaking the groves of <s>kadamba</s>, <s>sarja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, and <s>ketakī</s>,
fragrant with their blossoms,
cool from contact with the mist-laden clouds,
the breeze — whom does it not make eager?
With tresses hanging down to the hip,
with fragrant flowers worn behind the ear,
with breasts [adorned] with necklaces, with faces [graced] with wine —
women arouse passion in their lovers.
They flow, they rain, they trumpet, they shine,
they spread, they dance, they take refuge —
the rivers, clouds, maddened elephants, forest interiors,
the beloved-bereft, the peacocks, the monkeys.
Clouds adorned with lightning-creepers and <s>Indra</s>'s bow,
rain-clouds hanging heavy with their load of water,
and women blazing with golden girdles and jeweled earrings —
both captivate the hearts of travelers at once.
Garlands fashioned of fresh <s>kadamba</s>-stamens and <s>ketakī</s> [flowers],
women today wear upon their heads,
and behind their ears, ornaments fashioned as desired
from sprays of the <s>kububha</s> tree.
Their limbs anointed with fine <s>aguru</s> (aloe) and sandal-paste,
their tresses made fragrant with flower-ornaments,
hearing the rumble of rain-clouds, at dusk,
women quickly enter the bedchamber from their elders' house.
Dark blue as petals of <s>kuvalaya</s> lotuses, lofty, bowing with rain,
stirred by soft breezes, swaying slowly, gently,
the rain-clouds with their <s>Indra</s>-bows
steal away the minds of travelers' wives, tormented by separation.
As if delighted with <s>kadamba</s> trees in bloom all around,
as if dancing with trees whose branches sway in the wind,
as if laughing with the needle-like [buds] of <s>ketakī</s> flowers —
the forest interior, its heat broken by the sprinkling of new rain [appears thus].
A garland of <s>bakula</s> mixed with <s>mālatī</s> for the head,
and buds of <s>yūthikā</s> in bloom with fresh flowers,
and fresh <s>kadamba</s> blossoms for the women's ear-ornament —
this season arranges [them] like a lover, [giving] the rain in abundance.
With fine upraised breast-tips bearing necklace-strands,
with thin white silk on broad hip-circles,
with a line of body-hair risen from the sprinkling of fresh rain-drops,
and with gracefully-creased waist-regions — [such are] the women.
Cool from contact with fresh rain-drops,
the dancer for the trees bending under their load of blossoms,
fragrant with the pollen of <s>ketakī</s> flowers,
the wind steals the hearts of those whose beloveds are away.
'This is our refuge!' — [as if saying this,] the rain-clouds, bowed with water,
drenching with water, bending low with their load of rain,
seem to refresh the <s>Vindhya</s> [mountains],
scorched by the excessively harsh flames of summer-fire.
Delightful in many ways, captivating the minds of beautiful women,
a friend to trees, creepers, and branches, itself unchanging,
this rainy season, the very life-breath of living beings,
may it grant you blessings and the fulfillment of desires.
Third Canto
Clad in <s>kāśa</s>-grass garments, with a face lovely as an open lotus,
with the charm of ankle-bells [sounding like] maddened wild geese,
with a slender body bowed like ripened rice,
autumn has arrived, beautiful in form, like a new bride.
By <s>kāśa</s> grasses the earth, by the cool-rayed moon the nights,
by swans the river-waters, by <s>kumuda</s> (white night-lotuses) the lakes,
by <s>saptacchada</s> trees bending under their load of blooms the forests,
and the gardens by <s>mālatī</s> — all are made white.
With rows of darting, charming <s>śapharī</s> fish as waist-girdles,
with lines of white geese stationed along the edges as necklaces,
with broad sandy banks as hip-regions,
the rivers flow gently, like proud, beautiful women.
Somewhere the sky is [adorned] by clouds — white as silver, conch-shells, and lotus-stalks —
that have shed their water and, by lightness, departed in hundreds,
moving with the speed of wind;
it looks like a king fanned by hundreds of <s>cāmara</s> (yak-tail) fans.
The sky, charming like a mass of split collyrium,
the earth reddened with <s>bandhūka</s>-flower pollen,
and the embankments covered with tracts of ripened <s>kalama</s> rice —

children.text: protkaṇṭhayanti na mano bhuvi kasya yūnaḥ
children.translated_text: whose heart, of what young man on earth, do these not make eager?
With its most beautiful branch-tips swayed by gentle breezes,
with tender leaf-tips soft from the abundance of blooming flowers,
its honey drunk by intoxicated black bees —
the <s>kovidāra</s> tree — whose heart does it not rend?
Wearing the chief jewels of the host of stars,
her moon-face freed from the veil of clouds,
wearing the spotless silk garment of moonlight, the night
grows day by day, like a young woman.
With wave-garlands stirred by the <s>kāraṇḍava</s> (water-birds),
with banks crowded with flocks of <s>kādamba</s> geese and <s>sārasa</s> cranes,
reddened by the pollen of lotuses,
the rivers, with the cries of swans, everywhere delight people.
A feast for the eyes, with captivating garlands of rays,
refreshing, showering cool spray and water,
the moon yet burns exceedingly the slender bodies of women
wounded by the arrows of separation from their husbands, poisoned [by grief].
Shaking the nets of rice bowing under the weight of grain,
Making the trees, bowed with blossoms, dance,
shaking the lotus pond with its fully-bloomed lotuses,
the wind forcibly agitates the minds of women.
Adorned with pairs of intoxicated swans,
decorated with clear, fully-bloomed lotuses and water-lilies,
with garlands of waves raised by the gentle morning breeze —
the lakes suddenly make the heart eager.
The bow of <s>Indra</s> (the rainbow) has vanished into the bellies of clouds,
lightning no longer flashes — that sky-banner;
cranes no longer fan the sky with the wind of their wings;
peacocks no longer gaze at the heavens with upraised faces.
<s>Madana</s> (Cupid), leaving the peacocks bereft of their dance performances,
now attends the swans with their sweet singing;
leaving <s>kadamba</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, and <s>sarjanīpa</s> trees,
the beauty of blossom-emergence has approached the <s>saptacchada</s> trees.
The groves — enchanting with the fragrance of <s>śephālikā</s> flowers,
resounding with flocks of birds resting peacefully,
with blue lotuses [resembling] the eyes of deer standing at the edges —
make the minds of men yearn.
The wind at dawn, repeatedly shaking <s>kahlāra</s> lotuses, day-lotuses, and night-lilies,
having attained an even greater coolness from contact with them,
makes [people] yearn exceedingly,
while scattering the dew-drops clinging to the tips of leaves.
The borderlands — their grounds covered with abundant ripened rice,
adorned with prosperous herds of cattle resting peacefully,
resounding with flocks of swans and <s>sārasa</s> cranes —
generate delight in people.
The graceful gait of women is surpassed by swans,
the moon-like radiance of their faces by blooming lotuses,
their intoxicating eyes by blue water-lilies,
and their lovely brow-play by slender waves.
The dark creepers, with new shoots bent under the weight of flowers,
steal the beauty of women's arms adorned with ornaments;
and the fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine), beautiful with <s>kaṅkelī</s> blossoms,
[steals] the moon-like radiance of their clear, tooth-revealing smiles.
Women fill their hair — dense, dark, with curled tips pulled tight —
with fresh <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) flowers,
and in their ears, alongside excellent golden earrings,
they place various blue lotuses.
With necklaces mixed with sandal-paste, [they adorn] the circles of their breasts;
with girdle-strings, their ample hips;
with tinkling anklets, their lotus-feet —
women, their minds delighted, adorn themselves today.
Of the lakes — strewn with blooming white water-lilies, frequented by royal swans,
beautified by water gleaming like emerald gems —
the heavens, free of clouds, strewn with moon and stars,
bear a beauty of surpassing loveliness [rivaling those lakes].
In autumn, the winds blow cool from contact with <s>kumuda</s> (night-lilies);
the quarters of the sky, free of cloud-masses, are charming;
the water is free of murkiness, the earth [free] of thick mud;
the sky [shines] with a moon of pure rays, variegated with stars.
Some young women — their hands lovely as lotuses, clasped with their lovers' —
their faces outshining the moon,
generally proceed to their homes, made fragrant with flowers,
having abandoned the melody of song due to the force of powerful desire.
Possessed of the grace of love's delight, gathered with their good companions,
they abundantly suggest the sport of the Unequal-arrowed One (<s>Anāṅga</s>, Cupid);
with incomparable lip-color, in the middle of the night,
young women with fresh lovers display their pleasures in autumn.
Pressed by the sun's rays at dawn,
the lotus — resembling a fair young woman's face — opens today;
and the night-lily, when the moon's orb has set, closes —
like the smile of brides whose beloveds are away.
Recognizing the beauty of his beloved's dark eyes in the blue lotuses,
the tinkling of her golden girdle in the calls of the intoxicated swans,
the lovely splendor of her lips in the <s>bandhujīva</s> flower,
the traveler now weeps, his mind bewildered.
Leaving the moon-like radiance in women's faces,
the desirable sound of swans in jeweled anklets,
the <s>bandhūka</s> radiance in charming lips —
the fortunate beauty of autumn's arrival departs to some [unknown] place.
With a face of blooming lotuses, eyes of full-blown blue water-lilies,
wearing garments white as blossomed fresh <s>kāśa</s>-grass,
with the charming radiance of night-lilies — like an intoxicated woman of desire —
may this autumn bestow the highest delight upon your hearts!
Fourth Canto.
Lovely with the emergence of new shoots and crops,
with <s>lodhra</s> trees in bloom, with ripened rice,
with lotuses vanished, with frost beginning to fall —
this early winter season (<s>hemanta</s>) has arrived.
With charming necklaces — white as sandal-paste,
as frost, <s>kunda</s> (jasmine), and the moon —
the circles of breasts of buxom women of pleasure
are no longer adorned [with such cool ornaments].
On the paired arms of women of pleasure,
bracelets and arm-bands no longer find a place;
nor fresh silk garments on the orbs of their hips,
nor thin fabrics on their full bosoms.
Women do not adorn their hips
with girdle-strings studded with variegated gold and gems,
nor their lotus-feet — possessing the beauty of lotuses —
with anklets that echo the sound of swans.
Women anoint their limbs with <s>kālīyaka</s> (black aloe),
their lotus-faces with decorative leaf-patterns,
their heads with the fragrance of dark aloe-wood incense —
for the festival of love-making.
Young women — their faces pale and wan from the exhaustion of love-sport,
having attained the arising of delight —
do not laugh aloud, [but rather] gaze at
their lips, bitten by teeth-tips and pressed [during passion].
Having encountered the beauty of women's full breasts and chests,
worn out from pressing against them,
the cold season, with frost drops clinging to grass-tips, falling,
cries out, as it were, at dawn.
The borderlands — strewn with abundant crops of rice,
adorned with herds of doe-eyed deer,
resounding enchantingly with the cries of <s>krauñca</s> (curlew) birds —
make the heart eager.
The lakes — adorned with blooming blue water-lilies,
decorated with intoxicated <s>kādamba</s> (geese),
with clear, delightfully cool water —
steal the hearts of men.
Seeing the road thoroughly drained of water,
[wives] bearing their husbands weary from travel,
gazed upon [longingly] by doe-eyed women,
seem to awaken [their] desires.
Ripening, constantly shaken
by winds made cold by frost,
the <s>priyangu</s> (millet) creeper, separated from her beloved,
turns pale, like a woman of pleasure.
With faces fragrant with the scent of flower-wine,
bodies perfumed by the warmth of [each other's] breath,
lying in mutual bodily embrace,
people sleep, pierced by the nectar of desire.
By their lips bearing the wounds and tooth-marks,
and breasts inscribed by fingertip scratches,
the merciless love-enjoyment of young women
in the bloom of youth is revealed.
One woman, mirror in hand, adorns
her lotus-face in the morning sunlight,
and pulling down her lip — whose essence was drunk by her lover,
bitten by his teeth-tips — she examines it.
Another, her body wearied by the exertion of abundant love-play,
her lotus-eyes reddened from the night's wakefulness,
her mass of hair disheveled and loosely falling from her drooping shoulders,
falls asleep, warmed by the gentle rays of the sun.
Removing from their heads the wilted garlands whose lovely fragrance has been enjoyed,
[they] with dense, dark tresses
and bodily grace bowed by the weight of full, uplifted breasts,
other young women arrange their hair.
Another, seeing her body enjoyed by her lover,
joyful, her lips arranged in beautiful radiance,
puts on her bodice, her limbs marked by nail-scratches,
with dangling dark, lovely curled locks, her eyes half-closed.
Others, having reached exhaustion from prolonged exertion
in the sport of love-play, their bodily grace relaxed,
the tips of their breasts bristling with horripilation,
beautiful women apply their unguents.
Charming in many ways, stealing the hearts of women,
with village borders busy with abundant ripened rice,
with frost falling, sung by the cries of <s>krauñca</s> birds —

children.text: pradiśatu himayuktaḥ kāla eṣaḥ sukhaṃ vaḥ
children.translated_text: may this frost-laden season bestow happiness upon you!
Fifth Canto.
The earth covered with grown rice and sugarcane fields,
made lovely here and there by the resounding cries of <s>krauñca</s> birds,
fully satisfying desire, dear to women —
hear, O beautiful-thighed one, of the season called <s>śiśira</s> (winter)!
The interiors of mansions with windows shut against the wind,
the fire, the rays of the sun,
heavy garments, young women in their prime —
these become the objects of people's service in this season.
Neither sandal-paste cool as moonbeams,
nor the terrace of a mansion pure as the autumn moon,
nor winds cold with dense frost
delight the hearts of people now.
Cold from the onslaught of masses of frost,
further chilled by the moon's rays,
adorned beautifully with clusters of pale stars —
the nights are not fit to be endured by people.
Having taken betel, unguents, and garlands,
their lotus-faces scented with flower-wine,
abundantly perfumed with the incense of dark aloe-wood —
women eagerly enter the bedchamber.
Seeing their husbands — who had committed offenses, threatened many times,
trembling, their minds robbed by apprehension —
now desirous of love-making,
the women joyfully forgot those offenses.
By youths fully desirous, mercilessly,
during the long nights, enjoyed for a long time,
their breasts moving slowly from the fatigue and weariness,
young women in the bloom of youth wander languidly at night's end.
With breasts compressed by lovely bodices,
their chests adorned with colored silken garments,
their hair set with flowers within —
women seem to adorn the winter season itself.
With breasts golden-tawny from saffron (<s>kuṅkuma</s>) paste,
pleasantly warm with the heat of fresh youth,
pressed to the chests of women of pleasure,
lovers sleep, conquering the cold.
With blue lotuses trembling from fragrant sighs,
enchanting, awakening the desire for love,
at night, delighted women, together with their lovers,
drink the finest wine, intoxicating.
One woman at dawn, her intoxicated flush of passion gone,
her breast-tips pressed tight by her husband's embrace,
gazing at her body enjoyed by her dearest lover,
goes from her sleeping garment to another dress, laughing.
Another woman of desire, bearing her mass of hair
fragrant with incense of aloe-wood, its flower-garland fallen, its tips curled,
with heavy hips, deep navel, slender waist —
leaves her bed at dawn, [displaying] beautiful radiance.
With face-orbs having lips beautifully copper-red, like golden lotuses,
with reddish outer corners of their eyes resting against their temples,
with hair clinging to their shoulders at dawn —
women stand within the house today like [embodiments of] <s>Śrī</s> (the goddess of beauty).
Burdened by the weight of their broad hips, slightly stooped at the waist,
walking slowly, slowly, from the weariness of their breast-weight,
swiftly discarding the attire of the nighttime love-encounter,
other young women don the dress suitable for daytime.
Gazing at the tips of their breasts marked with nail-scratches,
touching their lip-shoots bitten by teeth,
these young women delight in the memory of beloved love-play
and adorn their faces at the time of sunrise.
Abundant with preparations of jaggery, delightful with sweet rice and sugarcane,
with vigorous sports of love-play arousing the pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
a cause of heart-burning for those separated from their dear ones —
may this winter season always be for your welfare!
Sixth Canto [Description of Spring].
With sharp arrows of full-blown mango shoots,
with a bowstring splendid with garlands of bees,
to pierce the minds of those given to love-play —
the warrior Spring has arrived, O beloved!
Trees are in flower, water is with lotuses,
women are with desire, the wind is fragrant,
evenings are pleasant, and days are delightful —
everything is most charming in spring, O beloved!
With mansions made cool by a slight frost,
and lovely heads perfumed with <s>campaka</s> flowers,
in the spring season women adorn
their breasts with necklaces and enchanting blossoms.
Upon the waters of ponds, upon jeweled girdles,
upon the radiance of the moon, upon women,
upon mango trees laden with blossoms —
spring bestows good fortune.
With silken garments reddened by <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) dye,
the orbs of women's hips [are adorned];
with thin fabrics whitened by saffron (<s>kuṅkuma</s>) paste,
the circles of their breasts are decorated.
In their ears, the fitting fresh <s>karṇikāra</s> [flower],
in their waving dark locks, the <s>aśoka</s>,
and the full-blown flower of fresh <s>mallikā</s> (jasmine) —
these enhance the beauty of women.
Upon their breasts, necklaces moist with white sandal-paste;
upon their arms, bracelets and armlets find their place;
upon the hips of full-hipped women
whose minds are troubled by <s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) — girdles.
Upon the faces of women of pleasure —
adorned with decorative leaf-patterns, resembling golden lotuses —
the arrival of perspiration, charming with pearls between gems,
attains profusion.
Loosening the slack bindings of
their limbs agitated by <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
when their beloveds are nearby,
women become utterly eager.
Thin, pale, languid with intoxication,
constantly inclined to yawning,
<s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) renders the limbs of women
filled with the excitement of loveliness.
People desire the shade of trees,
and at night they wish for the moon's rays;
they go to the pleasant, cool terrace to sleep
and tightly embrace their beloved for coolness.
In the eyes — restless, in the intoxicated, languid [eyes];
in the cheeks — pale; in the breasts — firm;
in the waist — hollow; in the hips — full —
today <s>Anaṅga</s> (Cupid) dwells in manifold ways in women.
Limbs playful with the grace of drowsiness,
words somewhat languid with wine,
sidelong glances cast with a play of brows —
<s>Kāma</s> (desire) has fashioned these in the women.
Mixed with <s>priyangu</s>, <s>kālīyaka</s> (black aloe), and <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron),
upon their fair breasts, by women of pleasure,
sandal-paste is applied by the women
by women languid with passion, [bodies] anointed with musk —
Casting off heavy garments quickly,
thin ones, dyed with lac-juice,
perfumed with fragrant black <s>aguru</s> (aloe) incense —
people wear [these], their limbs languid with the intoxication of desire.
The male <s>kokila</s> (cuckoo), intoxicated by the nectar-wine of mango juice,
kisses his beloved, thrilled with passion;
and this one, stationed on a lotus, with buzzing bees,
makes sweet flattery to the beloved of his beloved.
With clusters of copper-red new shoots bending them down,
the mango trees, with beautifully blossoming branches,
shaken by the wind, fill with desire
the restless minds of women.
Crimson from root [to crown] like coral,
bearing masses of blossoms along with new shoots,
the <s>aśoka</s> trees make sorrowful the hearts
of young women in the bloom of youth, when gazed upon.
With beautiful flowers kissed by intoxicated bees,
with soft new shoots bending in the gentle breeze —
the <s>atimukta</s> (Hiptage) creepers, when beheld, suddenly
arouse longing in the minds of lovers.
The splendor of the <s>kurabaka</s> tree's flower-clusters,
recently arisen, graced by the lustre of beloved's faces —
seeing them, whose heart among the tender-hearted
is not wounded by the fall of <s>Kandarpa's</s> (Love's) arrows, O beloved?
With <s>kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) groves everywhere, shaken by the wind,
bowing with blossoms, resembling blazing fire,
the earth, suddenly adorned by the spring season,
shines like a new bride wearing a red garment.
What has not been split by the <s>kiṃśuka</s> flowers, colored like parrot-beaks?
What has not been burnt by the <s>karṇikāra</s> blossoms?
That this <s>kokila</s> again, with its sweet words,
strikes the minds of young men fixed upon beautiful-faced women!
By male <s>kokilas</s> with sweet voices, delighted,
cooing, and by bees uttering intoxicated melodies —
the hearts of young brides, even in well-bred households,
modest and bashful, are in a moment made agitated.
Shaking the blossoming branches of mango trees,
spreading the <s>parabhṛta's</s> (cuckoo's) songs in all directions,
the wind blows, stealing the hearts of men —
delightful in spring, after the passing of frost-fall.
By <s>kunda</s> flowers, white as the laughter of a graceful young bride,
the groves are illuminated, charming to the mind —
they steal even the heart of a sage free from passion,
how much more the minds of young men stained with desire!
With hanging golden girdles, necklaces clinging to breasts,
their bodies' uprightness loosened by <s>Kandarpa's</s> pride,
in the month of <s>Madhu</s> (spring), with the sweet sounds of <s>kokilas</s> and bees,
women forcibly steal the hearts of men.
Adorned with trees bearing various delightful blossoms,
with mountain slopes alive with the joyful cries of well-fed [birds],
with rock surfaces enveloped by networks of mountain-creepers —
seeing the mountains, all people become filled with joy.
He closes his eyes, he weeps, he falls into grief,
he blocks his nose with his hand and wails aloud —
the traveler, his mind's activity tormented by separation from his beloved,
upon seeing the blossoming mango trees.
With the songs of intoxicated bees and <s>kokilas</s>,
with blossoming mango trees and <s>karṇikāras</s>, it is delightful —
the month of flowers pierces the minds of proud women
as if with sharp arrows, kindling <s>Manmatha</s> (Love).
The mango trees releasing heaps of blossoms of lovely golden lustre,
in bloom, shaken by the gentle breeze —
gazing directly at them, even emaciated on the road,
the traveler falls into a swoon from the blows of <s>Madana's</s> (Love's) arrows.
With the delightful, sweet songs of the <s>parabhṛta</s> (cuckoo) — [mocking] good speech;
with the lustre of <s>kunda</s> blossoms — [mocking] the rays of smiling teeth;
with new shoots like coral — [mocking] the beauty of their hand-buds —
the spring now mocks the women who are in love.
With faces like golden lotuses, with pale cheeks,
with necklaces placed above, with breast-tips moist with sandalwood,
with glances of passion-born grace, [these] women,
bending from the weight of their breasts, desire [even] the most tranquil lords among sages.
The lotus-face fragrant with <s>madhu</s> (honey/spring), eyes red as <s>lodhra</s>,
the hair, lovely and filled with fresh <s>kurabaka</s> [flowers],
the pair of heavy breasts, the hips likewise —
what of women now does not serve as [a weapon for] <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of Love)?
The hearts of steadfast women are shaken
by winds scented from blossoming mango trees,
by the calls of the love-maddened <s>parabhṛta</s>,
and by the pleasing singing sounds of bees.
The early evening is delightful, with bright moonlight;
the male <s>kokila's</s> song; the fragrant wind;
the humming of intoxicated bee-swarms; wine-drinking at night —
all this is an elixir for the Flower-Weaponed One (<s>Kāmadeva</s>).
Sweet-lipped like red <s>aśoka</s> [petals] imagined, sounding with intoxicated bee-hum,
with teeth pure-white like <s>kunda</s> garlands, with a face like a full-blown lotus,
with a wind gentle and fragrant with mango-blossom scent — the guru of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) initiation —

children.text: kalpāntaṃ madanapriyo diśatu vaḥ puṣpāgamo maṅgalam
children.translated_text: may the arrival of flowers, dear to <s>Madana</s>, bestow upon you auspiciousness until the end of the age!
Pierced by the <s>Malaya</s> (southern mountain) wind, charming with the <s>kokila's</s> song,
having obtained a continuous fragrance from the sprinkling of sweet honey,
encircled on all sides by swarms of various bees —
may the spring, the best of seasons, bring you happiness!
The mango with its lovely flower-cluster is his chosen arrow; the fine <s>kiṃśuka</s> is his bow;

children.text: jyā yasyālikulaṃ kalaṅkarahitaṃ chattraṃ sitāṃśuḥ sitam
children.translated_text: the host of bees is his bowstring; the spotless white moon is his white parasol;
the intoxicated elephant is the <s>Malaya</s> wind; the <s>parabhṛta</s> (cuckoo) is his captive [bard] — the Conqueror of the World (<s>Kāmadeva</s>),
he, accompanied by spring, may he spread blessings upon you widely!
